headline: Wetlands are Earth's kidneys—filtering water, absorbing floods, and nurturing life
universal_truth: The spaces between extremes often hold the greatest value
fun_facts: Wetlands cover only 6% of Earth's surface but host 40% of all species
One acre of wetland can store 1.5 million gallons of floodwater
We've destroyed over 50% of Earth's wetlands in the last century
discussion_questions: What transition zones or 'in-between' spaces do you undervalue?
How do wetlands demonstrate that neither extreme is always best?
What can we learn from ecosystems that thrive between two worlds?

hook.script: Not quite land, not quite water—wetlands exist in between. For centuries, we saw them as wastelands and drained them. Now we know the truth: wetlands are among Earth's most valuable ecosystems. They filter water, prevent floods, and burst with life.

cliff.script: Wetlands cover just 6% of Earth's land but support 40% of species. How does such a small area generate such extraordinary abundance? What makes these in-between places so productive?

options.text: The mix of water and land creates nutrient-rich conditions for diverse life
options.response: Yes. Where water meets land, nutrients concentrate and life explodes.

options.text: Species from both aquatic and terrestrial habitats overlap there
options.response: Overlap helps, but wetlands also create unique conditions...

fact1.title: Nature's Kidneys
fact1.script: Wetlands filter pollutants, trap sediment, and purify water. They're so effective that engineers now build artificial wetlands to treat wastewater. What we once drained as nuisance now inspires our best technology.

fact2.title: Flood Sponges
fact2.script: One acre of wetland can absorb 1.5 million gallons of floodwater. Wetlands act like sponges—absorbing excess water during storms, releasing it slowly during droughts. Every wetland we destroy increases flood damage downstream.

fact3.title: Biodiversity Hotspots
fact3.script: Wetlands host an astonishing proportion of species—fish, birds, amphibians, insects, plants. Many species can survive nowhere else. When we drain wetlands, we don't just lose water management—we lose irreplaceable life.

wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: The spaces between extremes are often the richest. Wetlands thrive precisely because they're neither pure land nor pure water. Life often flourishes most in the transitions, the boundaries, the places that don't fit neat categories.

outro.script: That's Day 62. Tomorrow, we'll explore cities under the sea—coral reefs. Until then, appreciate the in-between spaces in your life.

growTrack.title: In-Between Spaces - Value the Transitions
growTrack.learning_objective: Recognize value in transitional spaces and states
growTrack.activity: Identify an 'in-between' space in your life—a transition period, a role that spans two worlds, a place that's neither one thing nor another. How might this transition zone be more valuable than the extremes on either side?
